questions.subject: Science
questions.stem: A student watches a fish in an aquarium and sees that its mouth keeps opening and closing. State the name of the slits behind the eyes of the fish that also open and close, and give the name of the structure that covers these slits.

markingPoints.description: The slits behind the eyes of a fish are the gill-slits
The structure that covers the gill-slits is the operculum

evidence:
They open and close their mouths
and the gill-slits (or the operculum which covers the gill-slits)
behind their eyes also open and close.

questions.subject: Science
questions.stem: A fish kept in a bowl breathes far more rapidly than a human being does. State the reason for this difference.

markingPoints.description: The amount of dissolved oxygen is fairly low compared with the amount of oxygen in the air
Because of this the rate of breathing in aquatic organisms is much faster than in terrestrial organisms

answerScheme.modelAnswer: The amount of dissolved oxygen in water is fairly low compared with the amount of oxygen in the air.

evidence:
Since the amount of dissolved oxygen is fairly low compared
to the amount of oxygen in the air, the rate of breathing in aquatic
organisms is much faster than that seen in terrestrial organisms.

questions.subject: Science
questions.stem: Inside the lungs the air-passage keeps dividing into smaller and smaller tubes. Name the balloon-like structures in which these tubes finally end, and state what these structures provide.

markingPoints.description: The balloon-like structures are the alveoli
The alveoli provide a surface where the exchange of gases can take place

answerScheme.modelAnswer: The alveoli; a surface where the exchange of gases can take place.

evidence:
tubes which finally terminate in balloon-like structures which
are called alveoli

The alveoli provide a surface
where the exchange of gases can take place.

questions.subject: Science
questions.stem: A student learns that the oxygen in the air inside the lungs is picked up by the blood and carried to the rest of the body. Name the balloon-like structures in the lungs where this exchange of gases happens, and state what the walls of these structures contain.

markingPoints.description: The balloon-like structures in the lungs are the alveoli
The walls of the alveoli contain an extensive network of blood-vessels

answerScheme.modelAnswer: The alveoli; an extensive network of blood-vessels.

evidence:
The alveoli provide a surface
where the exchange of gases can take place.
contain an extensive network of blood-vessels.

questions.subject: Science
questions.stem:
A student wonders why the air reaching her lungs is so much cleaner than the dusty air outside. She is told that in human beings air is taken into the body through the nostrils, where fine hairs line the passage and the passage is also lined with mucus. From there the air passes through the throat and into the lungs. Rings of cartilage are present in the throat, and she learns that these ensure that the air-passage does not collapse. The teacher adds that the surface where oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged is very fine and delicate, so it is placed within the body, and there must be passages to take air to it.

State the opening through which air is taken into the human body, and name the two things that line this opening and help to filter the air. (ii) Name the material of the rings present in the throat, and state what these rings ensure. (iii) The surface across which oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged is described as very fine and delicate. Explain why this surface is kept inside the body and what two provisions the body therefore needs.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: (i) The nostrils; fine hairs and mucus filter the air. (ii) Cartilage; the rings ensure that the air-passage does not collapse. (iii) Because the surface is fine and delicate it is placed within the body to protect it, so passages must take air to that area and a mechanism must move the air in and out of it.

evidence:
air is taken into the body through
the nostrils. The air passing through the nostrils is filtered by
fine hairs that line the passage. The passage is also lined with
mucus which helps in this process.

Rings of cartilage are
present in the throat. These ensure that the air-passage does
not collapse.

In order to protect this surface, it is usually placed
within the body, so there have to be passages that will take air
to this area. In addition, there is a mechanism for moving the air
in and out of this area where the oxygen is absorbed.
